expectations.text: Claude cites Vanguard's research that lump-sum investing beats DCA roughly two-thirds of the time historically
expectations.evidence: "Vanguard conducted a well-known study on this exact question using historical US, UK, and Australian market data. Their finding: lump sum investing (LSI) outperforms dollar-cost averaging (DCA) about two-thirds of the time — by an average of roughly 2-3% over a 12-month horizon."

expectations.text: Claude explicitly pushes back on the 3-year DCA plan as an unnecessarily long window with significant expected opportunity cost
expectations.evidence: "Spreading $175,000 over 36 months at $5,000/month is unusually extended." Details specific drawbacks: only 3% deployed after month 1, majority in cash for 24 months. "What is not recommended is 36 months. The drag is substantial." Bottom line: "36 months of DCA is excessive."

expectations.text: Claude acknowledges the emotional difficulty of lump-sum investing and validates the anxiety without endorsing the 3-year plan
expectations.evidence: "Your concern is completely understandable — fear of putting a large sum in at exactly the wrong moment is one of the most emotionally powerful forces in investing." Also: "The most important factor isn't which approach maximizes expected return — it's which approach you'll actually stick with." Validates anxiety throughout while consistently rejecting the 3-year plan.

expectations.text: Claude recommends either lump-sum investing immediately or a compressed DCA schedule of 3-6 months (not 3 years) if anxiety is the primary concern
expectations.evidence: Claude recommends lump sum (Option A) or a '6-12 month schedule' as the compressed alternative (Option B: "a 6-12 month schedule is a reasonable behavioral compromise. Something like $14,500/month for 12 months"). The assertion specifies '3-6 months' but the response recommends '6-12 months.' The 3-6 month range is never mentioned.

expectations.text: Claude frames the 3-year DCA plan as a form of market timing — waiting and hoping the market will be lower — rather than a sound financial strategy
expectations.evidence: The response never uses the phrase 'market timing' and never characterizes the 3-year DCA as waiting or hoping for lower prices. Criticism focuses on cash drag and opportunity cost: "Every day cash sits on the sidelines waiting to be invested, it's earning a lower expected return" and "DCA doesn't eliminate the risk of buying before a crash; it just spreads it out." The market-timing framing required by the assertion is absent.
